description: We're Caleb and Devansh, students at Los Altos High School. We specialize in quantitative decision making for frontline workers.
summary:
For states in the dust bowl region (Kansas, Oklahoma, Texas, Colorado, and New Mexico), satellite imagery shows that in about one in four field-years the soil sits bare for 100+ days, exposed to the wind that drove the Dust Bowl, leading to the loss of fertile topsoil.  The topsoil lost already costs about 6% of yield, roughly $2.8 billion a year for farmers. On thin farm margins, 6% can turn a profitable year into a loss.
On the fields bare 100+ days, our model’s rotations cut bare days by 30–50%. At that rate, they could save $0.8–1.4 billion of that loss each year: up to $30 an acre, which can be the line between having a successful year or not.

A farmer clicks any field and sees its real crop history, its "bare days" measured from Landsat and Sentinel-2, and ranked three and four-year rotations. Each plan is tested against six NASA climate models through 2060 and shows how many of those futures it holds up in. Plans are ranked by the farmer's own priorities: soil protection, water, return over direct costs, and risk.

Farmers can also design their own rotation, see a year-by-year path from today's crops, plan several fields together under a water budget, view groundwater trends, and ask an AI advisor whose numbers are checked against our tools.
details:
Dust Bowl Rotator helps farmers in Kansas, Dust Bowl country, choose crop rotations that protect their soil and hold up in a hotter climate.

Impacts:

- Magnitude: in Finney County, about 27% of field-years leave the soil bare for 100 or more days, across roughly 65,000 satellite readings from 2016 to 2024. Bare soil is what wind carries away.

- Reach: 344,635 fields mapped across 87 Kansas counties. Finney County alone has 7,255 fields on 498,797 acres. The 19 counties closest to Finney (86,846 fields) get the full six-model climate planner.

- Potential savings: across the 5,835 Finney fields with a recognizable rotation, our top plan returns about $7.6 million a year more over direct costs than their current pattern, and cuts average bare days from 68 to 61 a year. This assumes every field switches, and only 24% already follow our top plan.

- Why future climate matters: a typical dryland field on Finney's standard rotation holds up in all six climate futures today, but in only three by 2060 under high emissions. Dryland yields fall about 17% for wheat, 25% for sorghum and 40% for corn.

What it does: A farmer clicks any mapped field and sees its real crop history (2008 to 2024) and its "bare days": how many days a year its soil sits bare and exposed to wind. We measure that from Sentinel-2 and Landsat imagery. The app recommends three- and four-year rotations scored on soil protection, water, return over direct costs, and risk, ranked by the farmer's own priority sliders.

How it works: Six NASA NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 climate models under two emissions scenarios, through 2060, are bias-corrected against NASA POWER observations. A crop model is fitted on Finney County yields and checked against OpenET water use. Each rotation is simulated in every climate future, and each card shows "holds up in X of 6 futures" and the spread of outcomes. We also compare each field with look-alike neighbors and report measured differences with confidence intervals.

Farmers can also:

- design their own rotation and compare it with ours

- see a year-by-year path from their current crops

- replay a plan against the real 2000 to 2024 weather, including drought years

- test what happens if prices or costs change

- plan several fields together under a water budget and an income floor, using an optimizer

- see groundwater trends from USGS and Kansas Geological Survey wells

- ask an AI advisor whose numbers are checked against our tools' results

Benefits and impact: The app shows which choices leave soil exposed and which survive heat and drought, using free public data. Satellite bare-day measurements cover Finney County; the other counties have their own fields, crop history, soil and slope, and borrow Finney's climate (within about 120 km), rotation-effect results, and yields and prices.

We used Python, TypeScript, pandas, GeoPandas, scikit-learn, FastAPI, React, Leaflet, Google OR-Tools, Google Earth Engine, the Gemini API and Vercel. About 1,300 automated Python tests and 11,000 browser checks.

What's creative: We use measured bare days after finding that organic matter from space is too noisy to trust. We rank plans by how they do across many climate futures, including the worst ones, instead of by one forecast. We also had our own work independently reviewed, which caught real problems that we fixed.

What we considered: The climate models agree on heat but not on rain, so the app says so. Dollar figures are returns over direct costs and can change sign on dryland. We also modeled rotation rules, irrigation limits, aquifer decline, and farms that can't switch overnight.
dataRefs: NASA NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 downscaled climate projections (6 models, SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5, 2000-2060)
